extracted.intended_audience: members of the public, stakeholders, policy analysts, and economists who want to write public-interest regulatory comments using economic analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing public-interest notice-and-comment submissions that use economic analysis to evaluate proposed federal regulations, align with agency mandates, and increase influence on rulemaking. Emphasizes procedural knowledge, legal constraints, analytic topics, tone, and dissemination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the regulatory process
rubrics_metrics.description: Know how Congress delegates authority to agencies and the procedures agencies must follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track developing regulations via the Unified Agenda of Federal Regulatory and Deregulatory Actions (published biannually) but also monitor multiple other sources because not all developing regulations appear in the Agenda. Understanding process timing and procedural steps helps target comments effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the agency's public-interest definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Align arguments with how regulators interpret their mandate and define the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame analyses and recommendations so they are relevant to the agency's statutory responsibilities and policy objectives; tailoring arguments to the agency's conception of the public interest increases persuasive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master economic analysis topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and address the key subjects regulatory economists should examine when evaluating a proposed rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide highlights several core analytic topics (market failure analysis, baseline scenarios, alternative comparisons, distributional impacts) that commenters should understand and be prepared to evaluate or provide evidence about.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market failure analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the agency has correctly identified the relevant market failure (or whether a market failure exists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probe the agency's characterization of market failures, offer alternative explanations where appropriate, and provide evidence (theoretical and empirical) showing whether the alleged market failure justifies regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baseline scenarios
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine and critique the baseline (the counterfactual of what would happen absent the rule) used in the agency's analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the chosen baseline is realistic and supported by evidence; consider alternative baselines and their implications for estimated benefits and costs. Baseline choice can substantially change net benefits estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative comparisons and less-restrictive alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider and evaluate alternatives to the proposed regulation, especially less-restrictive or more cost-effective options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the proposed rule to plausible alternatives, including regulatory and non-regulatory options, and assess relative costs, benefits, and feasibility. Highlight whether the agency considered (or omitted) less-restrictive alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributional impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze how the costs and benefits of the rule are distributed across affected groups or populations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide or critique evidence on heterogeneous effects and distributional consequences (who bears costs, who receives benefits), and discuss equity or incidence concerns that may be relevant to the agency's decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize legal constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand statutory authority, limits on agency action, and other legal constraints that shape what a rule can lawfully do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether the proposed rule exceeds statutory authority or conflicts with legal limits; tie economic critiques to legal constraints where relevant to strengthen persuasive force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate format and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare comments that are substantive, professional, and written in proper style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid rhetoric and invective; present clear, well-documented arguments with transparent methods, citations, and readable organization. Professional tone and proper formatting increase credibility and likelihood of uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Share your work
rubrics_metrics.description: Distribute your comment and underlying analysis to interested stakeholders so others can build on or echo it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circulate findings and data to advocacy groups, researchers, and policymakers to amplify impact; sharing enables coordination and increases chances that influential actors will reference or repeat your analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be constructive and information-rich; support claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A constructive, information-rich comment that clearly communicates and supports its claims is more likely to have an impact than rhetorical objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on probing the agency's analysis (e.g., whether it identified the right market failure, used the right baseline, and considered less-restrictive alternatives). Provide evidence, transparent calculations, and clear explanations rather than mere criticism.
